% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Scope}

This document (\texttt{EWAS-HSB-SSEG-TRS-03}) is the Level-2 \textbf{Technical Requirements Specification (\abbr{TRS})} governing Configuration Item \textbf{\texttt{CI-03}: Space Segment (\abbr{SSEG}, \abbr{WBS} Element \texttt{123456.03})} of the \textbf{Early Warning Alarm System (\abbr{EWAS})}. Prepared in strict conformance with \textbf{ECSS-E-ST-10C} (\textbf{AD-02}) and \textbf{ECSS-E-ST-10-06C Annex A} (\textbf{AD-03}), this specification establishes the complete, frozen set of technical requirements necessary to design, manufacture, integrate, verify, launch, commission, operate, and dispose of the \abbr{EWAS} Space Segment as an integrated system element.

The scope of this \abbr{TRS} encompasses all space-borne elements of the two-segment \abbr{EWAS} architecture, specifically:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Hybrid Orbital Constellation Architecture:} The coordinated astrodynamic configuration, orbital slot allocation, multi-plane phasing, and coverage availability of the dual-tier constellation comprising \textbf{six (6) Geostationary Earth Orbit (\abbr{GEO}) detection satellites (\texttt{SATG})} operating at 35,786~km altitude (spaced uniformly at $60^\circ$ longitude intervals) and \textbf{seventy-two (72) Low Earth Orbit (\abbr{LEO}) tracking satellites (\texttt{SATL})} deployed at 1,000~km circular altitude in a high-inclination ($78^\circ\text{--}82^\circ$) Walker Delta $72/8/1$ pattern (8 orbital planes with 9 satellites per plane), satisfying top-level constellation requirements \texttt{R-005} through \texttt{R-008} of \textbf{AD-01}.
    \item \textbf{Space Segment Mission Chain and Latency Allocations:} The functional and performance allocations governing boost-phase Short-Wave/Medium-Wave Infrared (\abbr{SWIR}/\abbr{MWIR}) plume detection, real-time onboard proton-despiking and false-alarm filtering (\texttt{R-009}, \texttt{R-010}, \texttt{R-019}--\texttt{R-022}), immediate candidate-event reporting from \abbr{GEO} to the Ground Segment (\texttt{R-042}), reception of Ground Segment tracking commands (\texttt{R-043}, \texttt{R-044}), agile payload optical Line-of-Sight (\abbr{LOS}) acquisition within $< 5\text{ s}$ and pointing stabilization $< 2\text{ arcsec/s}$ by two selected \abbr{LEO} spacecraft (\texttt{R-024}), synchronized stereoscopic tracking, inter-satellite exchange of timestamped \abbr{LOS} vectors to compute an onboard preliminary 3D trajectory estimate (\texttt{R-023}), and encrypted downlink of both the timestamped stereoscopic \abbr{LOS} observation packages (with covariance metadata) and onboard preliminary trajectory estimate to the Ground Segment Data Processing System for authoritative multi-sensor fusion (\texttt{R-012}, \texttt{R-026}, \texttt{R-027}, \texttt{R-045}) within the Space Segment's allocated share of the $\le 60\text{ s}$ end-to-end warning latency budget (\texttt{R-011}).
    \item \textbf{Mandatory Space Segment Inter-Satellite Link (\abbr{ISL}) Network:} The optical and radio-frequency (\abbr{OISL}/\abbr{RF} \abbr{ISL}) mesh across the 72 \abbr{LEO} nodes and the cross-layer \abbr{GEO}--\abbr{LEO} relay links connecting \texttt{SATL} and \texttt{SATG}, together with cryptographic security (\texttt{R-031}), anti-jamming resilience (\texttt{R-032}), and near-real-time telemetry/command transport (\texttt{R-033}, \texttt{R-044}).
    \item \textbf{Standardized Platform Envelopes, Environment, and Sustainability:} Common platform and subsystem boundaries under the project's \textbf{``Careful \abbr{COTS}'' / Radiation-Tolerant \abbr{COTS}} philosophy, explicitly covering the \emph{Structures and Mechanisms Subsystem (\abbr{STR/MEC})} (including stray-light baffles per \texttt{R-025}, micro-vibration isolation, rideshare dispenser interfaces, and localized \textrm{Al}/\textrm{Ta} radiation spot shielding), \emph{Thermal Control Subsystem (\abbr{TCS})}, \emph{Attitude Determination and Control Subsystem (\abbr{ADCS})}, \emph{Electrical Power Subsystem (\abbr{EPS})}, \emph{Propulsion Subsystem (\abbr{PROP})}, and the architecturally separated \emph{On-Board Data Handling (\abbr{OBDH})} and \emph{Communications (\abbr{TT\&C}/\abbr{ISL})} subsystems, designed for operational lifetimes of 7~years (\abbr{LEO}) and 15~years (\abbr{GEO}) (\texttt{R-016}) and mandatory active end-of-life disposal (\texttt{R-018}, \textbf{AD-12}).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Position in the EWAS Specification Tree and Hierarchy}

Per \textbf{ECSS-E-ST-10C} Clause 5.2 (\textbf{AD-02}), the \abbr{EWAS} technical documentation is organized into a hierarchical specification tree aligned with the project Work Breakdown Structure (\abbr{WBS}, Chapter 10 of \textbf{AD-01}):
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Upper-Tier Parent Baseline (Level 1 --- System Level):} This \abbr{TRS} flows down directly from the \emph{EWAS Overall System Requirements} (\texttt{R-001} through \texttt{R-049}, Chapter 5 of \textbf{AD-01}), the \emph{Concept of Operations} (Chapter 3 of \textbf{AD-01}), and the \emph{Functional Analysis} (Chapter 6 of \textbf{AD-01}). Every technical requirement specified in Section 7 of this document maintains explicit backward traceability to one or more system-level requirements in \textbf{AD-01}.
    \item \textbf{Peer Segment Specifications (Level 2 --- Segment Level):} This document operates at the same hierarchical tier as the \emph{Ground Segment Technical Requirements Specification} (\abbr{WBS} Element \texttt{123456.02}) and is complemented by the \emph{Space Segment Design Definition File} (\texttt{EWAS-HSB-SSEG-DDF-03}), the \emph{Space Segment Design Justification File} (\texttt{EWAS-HSB-SSEG-DDJF-03}), and the segment-level \emph{Interface Control Documents} (\abbr{WBS} Elements \texttt{123456.05.02.01} through \texttt{123456.05.02.04}).
    \item \textbf{Subordinate Lower-Tier Specifications (Level 3 --- Spacecraft \& Subsystem Level):} This \abbr{TRS} defines requirements at the integrated Space Segment boundary (\texttt{123456.03 SSEG}) and establishes the top-level allocation envelopes for its two subordinate flight system Configuration Items: \textbf{Satellite \abbr{LEO} (\texttt{SATL}, \abbr{WBS} \texttt{123456.03.01})} and \textbf{Satellite \abbr{GEO} (\texttt{SATG}, \abbr{WBS} \texttt{123456.03.02})}. Detailed equipment-level and component-level procurement specifications for individual \texttt{SATL} and \texttt{SATG} hardware/software units are allocated to lower-tier subsystem specifications and are not duplicated herein unless required to guarantee cross-layer interoperability, constellation-level performance, or common environmental/product-assurance compliance.
\end{itemize}

\begin{table}[H]

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Purpose and Background}

The \textbf{Early Warning Alarm System (\abbr{EWAS})} is an interdisciplinary space systems engineering project developed jointly at \textbf{Hochschule Bremen (HSB)} and \textbf{Gdańsk University of Technology (Politechnika Gdańska --- PG)}. The mission is motivated by the acute security challenges facing the Baltic Sea region ($53^\circ\text{N}\text{--}66^\circ\text{N}$, $10^\circ\text{E}\text{--}32^\circ\text{E}$), where short flight times of short- and medium-range ballistic missiles (as well as longer-range threats originating outside the region, \texttt{R-049}) leave terrestrial radar networks with severely compressed reaction windows due to Earth-curvature horizon masking and terrain obstruction.

To overcome these physical limitations, \abbr{EWAS} establishes a sovereign, high-availability ($> 99.9\%$, \texttt{R-015}) space-based infrared observation and tracking architecture dedicated strictly to \textbf{civil protection, national crisis management, and emergency preparedness}. In accordance with \texttt{R-001} and \texttt{R-002}, \abbr{EWAS} is strictly a non-offensive early warning system: it does not provide weapon-guidance data, fire-control solutions, or interceptor command-and-control, nor is it required to perform final warhead yield characterization or post-impact damage assessment. Its core operational mandate is to detect ballistic missile launches during the high-radiance boost phase from Geostationary Earth Orbit (\abbr{GEO}), cue two suitable Low Earth Orbit (\abbr{LEO}) satellites via direct ground links or a \textbf{mandatory Space Segment Inter-Satellite Link (\abbr{ISL}) network} (\texttt{R-043}, \texttt{R-044}), execute rapid ($< 5\text{ s}$) optical Line-of-Sight (\abbr{LOS}) acquisition and synchronized stereoscopic tracking (\texttt{R-024}), compute an onboard preliminary 3D trajectory estimate via inter-satellite \abbr{LOS} vector exchange (\texttt{R-023}), and downlink both the timestamped stereoscopic \abbr{LOS} observation packages and preliminary trajectory estimate to the Ground Segment Data Processing System for authoritative multi-sensor fusion (\texttt{R-012}, \texttt{R-026}, \texttt{R-027}). Immediately following this authoritative two-\abbr{LEO} ground assessment, the Ground Segment Early Warning System automatically dispatches a preliminary warning to authorized national authority interfaces within a total end-to-end latency of $\le 60\text{ seconds}$ from initial \abbr{GEO} detection (\texttt{R-011}, \texttt{R-045}).

In compliance with Clause \texttt{<1>a} of \textbf{ECSS-E-ST-10-06C Annex A} (\textbf{AD-03}), the purpose and objective of this Technical Requirements Specification are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item To translate the system-level mission needs, operational scenarios, and requirements (\texttt{R-001} through \texttt{R-049} in \textbf{AD-01}) into unambiguous, quantifiable, attainable, and verifiable technical requirements for the \abbr{EWAS} Space Segment (\texttt{CI-03}, \abbr{WBS} \texttt{123456.03});
    \item To establish the technical reference baseline for the qualification of the Space Segment design (\texttt{EWAS-HSB-SSEG-DDF-03} and \texttt{EWAS-HSB-SSEG-DDJF-03}) and for formal verification and acceptance testing (\textbf{AD-04}, \textbf{AD-05}); and
    \item To define the permissible functional, physical, environmental, operational, and sustainability boundaries governing the 6 \abbr{GEO} (\texttt{SATG}) and 72 \abbr{LEO} (\texttt{SATL}) spacecraft throughout their complete life profile, from on-ground cleanroom integration through 7-year (\abbr{LEO}) and 15-year (\abbr{GEO}) nominal operations to active end-of-life disposal (\texttt{R-016}, \texttt{R-018}).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Normative Requirement Conventions and Identification Scheme}

In accordance with \textbf{ECSS-S-ST-00C} and \textbf{ECSS-E-ST-10-06C} Clauses 7.2.7 and 8.3 (\textbf{AD-03}), strict distinction is maintained between descriptive/informative text (Sections 1 through 6) and normative binding provisions (Section 7):
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{\texttt{shall}:} Expresses a mandatory technical requirement that is contractually and technically binding on the Space Segment design and subject to formal verification per \textbf{ECSS-E-ST-10-02C} (\textbf{AD-04}).
    \item \textbf{\texttt{should}:} Expresses a non-mandatory recommendation or engineering design target where alternative solutions may be justified in the Design Justification File (\texttt{EWAS-HSB-SSEG-DDJF-03}).
    \item \textbf{\texttt{may}:} Expresses a permissible practice or optional allowance within the specified boundaries.
    \item \textbf{\texttt{can}:} Expresses a physical possibility or inherent capability of an element.
    \item \textbf{\texttt{will}} (or indicative present tense): Expresses a descriptive statement of fact, background context, or external interface condition not subject to Space Segment verification.
\end{itemize}

Furthermore, in compliance with \textbf{ECSS-E-ST-10-06C} Clause 8.3.3, ambiguous, unverifiable, or open-ended terms (such as \emph{``and/or''}, \emph{``etc.''}, \emph{``optimize''}, \emph{``minimize''}, \emph{``maximize''}, \emph{``rapid''}, \emph{``sufficient''}, \emph{``adequate''}, or \emph{``state of the art''}) are strictly excluded from the normative requirement statements in Section 7. Every technical requirement in Section 7 is assigned a unique, persistent identifier following the taxonomy:
\[
\texttt{SSEG-REQ-<CAT>-<NNN>}
\]
where \texttt{SSEG} denotes Configuration Item \texttt{CI-03} (Space Segment), \texttt{REQ} denotes a normative technical requirement, \texttt{<NNN>} is a sequential three-digit number (\texttt{001}, \texttt{002}, \dots), and \texttt{<CAT>} identifies the functional or ECSS requirement category summarized below:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{\texttt{FUN} / \texttt{MIS} / \texttt{PERF}:} Functional (\texttt{FUN}), Mission \& Constellation Geometry (\texttt{MIS}), and System Performance \& Latency (\texttt{PERF}) requirements.
    \item \textbf{\texttt{PLD} / \texttt{ISL} / \texttt{ADCS} / \texttt{OBDH}:} Infrared Sensor Payload (\texttt{PLD}), Communications \& Mandatory Inter-Satellite Links (\texttt{ISL}), Attitude \& Agile \abbr{LOS} Steering (\texttt{ADCS}), and On-Board Data Handling (\texttt{OBDH}) requirements.
    \item \textbf{\texttt{STR} / \texttt{TCS} / \texttt{EPS} / \texttt{PROP}:} Structures \& Mechanisms (\texttt{STR}), Thermal Control (\texttt{TCS}), Electrical Power (\texttt{EPS}), and Propulsion \& End-of-Life Disposal (\texttt{PROP}) requirements.
    \item \textbf{\texttt{IF} / \texttt{ENV} / \texttt{OPS} / \texttt{PA} / \texttt{VER}:} External Interfaces (\texttt{IF}), Space \& Launch Environment (\texttt{ENV}), Operational Modes \& Autonomy (\texttt{OPS}), Product Assurance \& ``Careful \abbr{COTS}'' (\texttt{PA}), and Verification (\texttt{VER}) requirements.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{3. User's Need Presentation}

In accordance with Clause \texttt{<3>} (\emph{User's need presentation}) of \textbf{ECSS-E-ST-10-06C Annex A} (\textbf{AD-03}), this section characterizes the operational security environment, end-user civil-protection needs, architectural allocation, and external interfaces that govern the \abbr{EWAS} Space Segment (\texttt{CI-03}, \abbr{WBS} Element \texttt{123456.03}) as a primary sensing and space-relay component of the overall \abbr{EWAS} system (\textbf{AD-01}).

\subsubsection{3.1 Operational Context, Threat Landscape, and Mission Need}

The \textbf{Baltic Sea region} (encompassing the sovereign territories, maritime exclusive economic zones, and critical population centers bounded approximately by latitudes $53^\circ\text{N}\text{--}66^\circ\text{N}$ and longitudes $10^\circ\text{E}\text{--}32^\circ\text{E}$) faces an increasingly volatile strategic security environment. A critical vulnerability of the region is its geographic proximity to potential launch corridors for Short-Range Ballistic Missiles (\abbr{SRBM}, range $< 1,000\text{ km}$, total flight times of 3--7~minutes) and Medium-Range Ballistic Missiles (\abbr{MRBM}, range 1,000--3,000~km, total flight times of 7--15~minutes), alongside Intermediate-Range and Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles (\abbr{IRBM}/\abbr{ICBM}) launched from outside the immediate Baltic theatre whose trajectories may threaten Baltic states (\texttt{R-049}).

Conventional early warning postures relying exclusively on ground-based radar installations suffer from fundamental physical and geometric limitations in this theatre:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Earth-Curvature Horizon Masking:} Due to the curvature of the Earth, a terrestrial radar with an antenna height of $h_r \approx 30\text{ m}$ cannot achieve line-of-sight visibility to an ascending missile until the vehicle clears the local radar horizon $d_h \approx 4.12\bigl(\sqrt{h_r} + \sqrt{h_t}\bigr)$ (in km, for altitudes in meters). At typical regional stand-off distances of 400--800~km, an ascending threat missile remains masked below the radar horizon throughout its initial boost phase (altitudes below 15--45~km), delaying initial detection by 60--150~seconds after rocket motor ignition.
    \item \textbf{Terrain Obstruction, Atmospheric Clutter, and Depressed Trajectories:} Forested topography, maritime ducting, and quasi-ballistic depressed trajectories further degrade low-elevation ground radar acquisition, leaving national civil-protection authorities with insufficient lead time to execute public sheltering and infrastructure protection protocols.
\end{itemize}

To eliminate this horizon-masking blind spot, end users---specifically \textbf{Authorized National Crisis-Management Authorities, Ministries of the Interior, and Emergency Warning Centers} across the Baltic partner states (Chapter 8 of \textbf{AD-01})---require a persistent, space-based early warning capability that detects ballistic missile launches at the earliest physically observable stage: \textbf{rocket motor ignition and boost-phase ascent} (\texttt{R-007}, \texttt{R-009}). During the boost phase (typically lasting 45--180~seconds depending on missile class), propellant combustion releases megawatts of radiant intensity in the Short-Wave Infrared (\abbr{SWIR}) and Medium-Wave Infrared (\abbr{MWIR}) spectral bands, providing a high-contrast radiometric signature observable from orbit above cloud tops.

To translate space-based boost-phase detection into actionable civil-protection lead time, the user need imposes three overarching system drivers on \abbr{EWAS}:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Automated Preliminary Warning within $\le 60\text{ Seconds}$ (\texttt{R-011}, \texttt{R-045}):} The elapsed time from the first Geostationary Earth Orbit (\abbr{GEO}) detection of a candidate launch event to the automated delivery of a preliminary warning product at the authorized national authority interface must not exceed \textbf{60~seconds}. Within this 60-second window, the system cannot rely solely on coarse single-tier \abbr{GEO} coordinates; the warning may be issued \textbf{only after} two selected Low Earth Orbit (\abbr{LEO}) satellites have acquired follow-on stereoscopic observations and the Ground Segment has fused those observations into a refined 3D trajectory and probabilistic impact-area (\textbf{Instantaneous Impact Point --- \abbr{IIP}}) estimate with explicit confidence ellipses (\texttt{R-012}, \texttt{R-013}, \texttt{R-045}).
    \item \textbf{Continuous 24/7 Surveillance and $> 99.9\%$ Availability (\texttt{R-006}, \texttt{R-008}, \texttt{R-010}, \texttt{R-015}):} The Space Segment must maintain uninterrupted temporal and spatial surveillance without coverage gaps over the protected region and surrounding launch corridors, achieving a launch detection probability $> 95\%$ (\texttt{R-010}) and contributing to an overall system operational availability $> 99.9\%$ (\texttt{R-015}) across 7-year (\abbr{LEO}) and 15-year (\abbr{GEO}) operational design lifetimes (\texttt{R-016}).
    \item \textbf{Strict Compliance with Non-Offensive Civil-Protection and Data Sovereignty Boundaries (\texttt{R-001}--\texttt{R-004}, \texttt{R-048}):} \abbr{EWAS} is conceived exclusively as a defensive civil-protection decision-support asset:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \emph{Non-Offensive Mandate (\texttt{R-001}):} The system is strictly prohibited from providing weapon targeting coordinates, fire-control solutions, interceptor mid-course guidance, or direct command of military kinetic response assets.
        \item \emph{Scope Limitation (\texttt{R-002}):} The system is not required to perform definitive missile-variant identification, warhead nuclear/conventional yield estimation, or post-impact battle damage assessment.
        \item \emph{Authorized Institutional Access \& Sovereign Archival (\texttt{R-003}, \texttt{R-004}, \texttt{R-034}--\texttt{R-037}, \texttt{R-047}, \texttt{R-048}):} Warning outputs are delivered exclusively to authorized governmental crisis-management interfaces (\texttt{R-003}), which form the external boundary of \abbr{EWAS} (downstream public siren/cell-broadcast activation remains the responsibility of national authorities per \texttt{R-048}). All archived telemetry and observation records are retained for at least 5~years (\texttt{R-036}) and restricted strictly to algorithm refinement, radiometric/geometric calibration, performance verification, operator training, and post-event technical analysis (\texttt{R-004}).
    \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{3.2 Role of the Space Segment in the Two-Segment EWAS Warning Chain}

Per Clause \texttt{<3>b--d} of \textbf{ECSS-E-ST-10-06C Annex A}, the Space Segment (\abbr{SSEG}, \abbr{WBS} \texttt{123456.03}) is not a standalone, self-contained product; it operates as one of the \textbf{two integrated system segments} that constitute the \abbr{EWAS} baseline (\textbf{AD-01}, Chapters 3 and 4):
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Space Segment (\abbr{SSEG}, \abbr{WBS} \texttt{123456.03}, \texttt{CI-03}):} The space-borne sensing, onboard processing, and inter-satellite relay infrastructure comprising the 6 \abbr{GEO} detection satellites (\texttt{SATG}, \abbr{WBS} \texttt{123456.03.02}) at 35,786~km and the 72 \abbr{LEO} tracking satellites (\texttt{SATL}, \abbr{WBS} \texttt{123456.03.01}) at 1,000~km, interconnected by a \textbf{mandatory Space Segment Inter-Satellite Link (\abbr{ISL}) network} (optical/\abbr{RF} \abbr{ISL} mesh across \abbr{LEO} and cross-layer \abbr{GEO}--\abbr{LEO} relay links).
    \item \textbf{Ground Segment (\abbr{WBS} \texttt{123456.02}):} The terrestrial infrastructure comprising the \emph{Data Archiving System} (\texttt{123456.02.01}), \emph{Command \& Control System} (\texttt{123456.02.02}), \emph{Mission Control Center} (\texttt{123456.02.03}), \emph{Data Processing System} (\texttt{123456.02.04}), \emph{Ground Station Network} (\texttt{123456.02.05}), and \emph{Early Warning System} (\texttt{123456.02.06}). External national crisis-management authorities are warning recipients connected to the Early Warning System interface, not a third system segment (\texttt{R-048}).
\end{enumerate}

To satisfy the $\le 60\text{-second}$ end-to-end latency requirement (\texttt{R-011}) from initial \abbr{GEO} detection to external national authority warning dispatch, the operational warning chain is partitioned into four deterministic steps across the Space and Ground Segments. Table~\ref{tab:warning_chain_latency} defines the functional sequence, segment responsibilities, exchanged data products (aligned with the Ground Segment Data Dictionary in Chapter 12 of \textbf{AD-01}), and binding latency budget allocations.

As shown in Table~\ref{tab:warning_chain_latency}, the Space Segment is directly responsible for \textbf{Steps 1 and 3} and provides the mandatory space-relay transport backbone for \textbf{Step 2}, representing a combined Space Segment latency allocation of $\le 40\text{--}45\text{ seconds}$. Two architectural mechanisms within \abbr{SSEG} are indispensable to closing this timing budget:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Mandatory Space Segment \abbr{ISL} Routing (\texttt{R-023}, \texttt{R-044}):} Because the two best-positioned \abbr{LEO} satellites over a launch corridor outside the Baltic region may not be in simultaneous line-of-sight of a European ground station at the instant of launch, relying solely on direct ground-station passes would introduce multi-minute store-and-forward delays, violating \texttt{R-011}. The mandatory \abbr{SSEG} \abbr{ISL} network (combining intra-/inter-plane optical/\abbr{RF} \abbr{ISL} mesh links across the 72 \abbr{LEO} satellites and cross-layer \abbr{GEO}--\abbr{LEO} trunks) guarantees continuous, sub-3-second command delivery (\texttt{R-044}), sub-second inter-satellite \abbr{LOS} vector exchange for onboard preliminary 3D trajectory computation (\texttt{R-023}), and immediate telemetry/observation return.
    \item \textbf{Agile Payload Optical \abbr{LOS} Steering without Full-Bus Slews (\texttt{R-024}):} Slewing an entire 1,000~km \abbr{LEO} spacecraft bus through $20^\circ\text{--}45^\circ$ using reaction wheels alone would require 15--30~seconds of settling time to reach arcsecond-class stability. By combining 3-axis spacecraft attitude control with a two-axis payload gimbal and high-bandwidth Fast Steering Mirror (\abbr{FSM}), each cued \texttt{SATL} node acquires and locks onto the target plume within $< 5\text{ seconds}$ while maintaining $< 2\text{ arcsec/s}$ \abbr{LOS} stability (\texttt{R-024}).
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{3.3 Space Segment System Boundaries and External Interfaces}

In accordance with Clause \texttt{<3>d} of \textbf{ECSS-E-ST-10-06C Annex A}, the boundary of Configuration Item \texttt{CI-03} (\abbr{SSEG}) is defined by four external interface categories connecting the flight constellation to the Ground Segment, the Launch Segment, the observable target/background environment, and regulatory/space-traffic entities. (Internal space-to-space \abbr{ISL} interfaces between \texttt{SATL} and \texttt{SATG} are internal to \abbr{SSEG} and are specified in Section 4 and Section 7.)     \thead{Interface ID} & \thead{Interface Name} & \thead{External Counterpart} & \thead{Principal Functional, Physical \& Protocol Characteristics} \\ \hline
    \textbf{IF-EXT-01} & Space-to-Ground \abbr{RF} \abbr{TT\&C} \& Mission Data Interface & Ground Station Network (\abbr{WBS} \texttt{123456.02.05}) \& Ground C2 (\texttt{123456.02.02}) & Bidirectional S-band/X-band \abbr{TT\&C} and high-rate X-band/Ka-band mission data downlinks; \abbr{CCSDS} packet/frame compliant (\textbf{RD-02}); NSA/EU-grade \abbr{COMSEC} encryption (\texttt{R-031}) and spread-spectrum anti-jamming/anti-spoofing protection (\texttt{R-032}, \texttt{R-033}). \\ \hline
    \textbf{IF-EXT-02} & Launch Vehicle \& Dispenser Interface & Launch Service Providers (Heavy-Lift \abbr{GEO} \& Medium/Heavy \abbr{LEO}) & Standard mechanical separation rings for \texttt{SATG}; multi-satellite rideshare dispenser mechanisms deploying 9~\texttt{SATL} spacecraft per plane; umbilical power/data/purge lines; launch fairing acoustic, vibrational, and quasi-static envelopes. \\ \hline
    \textbf{IF-EXT-03} & Target Plume \& Background Optical Interface & Boost/Post-Boost Missile Plumes \& Earth/Solar Background & Radiometric entrance aperture interface in \abbr{SWIR} ($\sim 2.7~\mu\text{m}$ $\text{H}_2\text{O}/\text{CO}_2$ band) and \abbr{MWIR} ($\sim 4.2\text{--}4.4~\mu\text{m}$ $\text{CO}_2$ red/blue spike bands); solar glint, Earth albedo, cloud-top thermal clutter, and stray-light rejection (\texttt{R-009}, \texttt{R-020}, \texttt{R-025}). \\ \hline
    \textbf{IF-EXT-04} & Space Traffic Management \& Regulatory Interface & Space Surveillance Networks \& \abbr{ITU} Radiocommunication Sector & Reception of Conjunction Data Messages (CDMs) via Ground C2 for collision avoidance at 1,000~km \abbr{LEO} and 35,786~km \abbr{GEO}; compliance with \abbr{ITU} frequency allocations (\textbf{RD-03}) and \textbf{ECSS-U-AS-10C} disposal (\texttt{R-018}, \textbf{AD-12}). \\ \hline
\end{tabularx}}
\end{table}

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Space-to-Ground Interface (\texttt{IF-EXT-01}: \abbr{SSEG} $\leftrightarrow$ Ground Segment \texttt{123456.02}):} Governs all radio-frequency (and future optical ground station) links between the 6 \texttt{SATG} and 72 \texttt{SATL} spacecraft and the Ground Station Network (\texttt{123456.02.05}), managed under the \emph{Space Segment Interface Control Document} (\abbr{WBS} \texttt{123456.05.02.04}) and \emph{Data Exchange ICD} (\texttt{123456.05.02.01}). The uplink carries authenticated telecommands, cryptographic key updates, ephemeris uploads, software patches, and \emph{LEO Tracking Requests} (\texttt{R-043}, \texttt{R-044}). The downlink carries spacecraft housekeeping telemetry, \emph{GEO Event Reports} (\texttt{R-042}), \emph{LEO Observation Packages} (timestamped stereoscopic \abbr{LOS} vectors with attitude/ephemeris covariance matrices), and \emph{Onboard Preliminary Trajectory} estimates (\texttt{R-023}). All links enforce end-to-end encryption (\texttt{R-031}), command authentication, and anti-jamming resilience (\texttt{R-032}).
    \item \textbf{Launch Segment Interface (\texttt{IF-EXT-02}: \abbr{SSEG} $\leftrightarrow$ Launch Vehicles):} Defines the mechanical, electrical, thermal, cleanliness, and dynamic load boundaries between the spacecraft Structures and Mechanisms Subsystem (\abbr{STR/MEC}) and commercial launch vehicles. For \texttt{SATG}, the interface supports single or dual-manifest geostationary transfer or direct \abbr{GEO} injection. For \texttt{SATL}, the interface is specifically engineered around modular multi-satellite dispenser rings capable of batch-injecting a complete orbital plane of 9 \abbr{LEO} satellites per launch into the 1,000~km, $78^\circ\text{--}82^\circ$ inclination orbit across 8 dedicated plane launches.
    \item \textbf{Target Plume and Background Optical Interface (\texttt{IF-EXT-03}: \abbr{SSEG} Payload $\leftrightarrow$ Radiometric Scene):} Defines the uncooperative optical boundary between the \abbr{SWIR}/\abbr{MWIR} telescope entrance pupils and the observed scene. The payload must discriminate high-temperature booster exhaust plumes (characterized by strong $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{CO}_2$ vibrational-rotational emission around $2.7~\mu\text{m}$ in \abbr{SWIR} and $4.2\text{--}4.4~\mu\text{m}$ in \abbr{MWIR}) against complex terrestrial and space backgrounds, including high-altitude solar reflections off cirrus clouds, sunlit limb scatter, industrial/wildfire thermal sources, and South Atlantic Anomaly (\abbr{SAA}) or polar proton transients (\texttt{R-019}--\texttt{R-022}, \texttt{R-025}).
    \item \textbf{Space Traffic Management and Regulatory Interface (\texttt{IF-EXT-04}):} Governs the operational interaction with international space situational awareness providers (via the Ground Segment Mission Control Center) for processing Conjunction Data Messages (CDMs) and executing collision-avoidance manoeuvres in the congested 1,000~km \abbr{LEO} regime, as well as adherence to International Telecommunication Union (\abbr{ITU}) spectral masks (\textbf{RD-03}), laser eye-safety/aviation-safety exclusions for optical links, and \textbf{ECSS-U-AS-10C} / \textbf{ESA Zero Debris} end-of-life disposal mandates (\texttt{R-018}, \textbf{AD-12}, \textbf{RD-01}).
\end{enumerate}
